text.en: Meena saved coins in a piggy bank. "Where do banks keep people's money?" she asked.

Money is anything accepted for payment. In early times people used barter, exchanging goods, which needed a double coincidence of wants. Money solved this problem. Today we use coins, notes and digital payments.
Banks keep savings safe and give loans. The Reserve Bank of India issues currency and controls the banking system. Banks pay interest on deposits and charge a higher interest on loans.
Credit means borrowing money, which can help, for example to start a business, but too much debt is risky. Self-help groups and cooperative societies give small loans to the poor, and in Tamil Nadu women's SHGs are strong.

Let us trace how money evolved over thousands of years. Before coins existed, communities used commodity money such as grain, cattle, shells or salt to trade.
Next came metallic money made of gold, silver and copper. Kings stamped their seals on coins to guarantee weight and purity, making long-distance trade far easier.
Carrying heavy bags of coins across kingdoms was risky, so paper currency emerged—backed by trust in the issuing authority rather than the metal value of the paper itself.
Today we also use plastic money such as debit and credit cards, and instant digital payments like UPI, NEFT and mobile wallets that transfer funds straight between bank accounts.

board.text: Modern money: cards & UPI digital payments

text.en: Economists describe four key functions of money: it is a medium of exchange, a measure of value, a store of value, and a standard for deferred payments like future loan repayments.
Why do people accept a hundred-rupee note? Because the Government of India declares it legal tender, and the Reserve Bank of India promises to honour its value.
Established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949, the Reserve Bank of India is India's central bank. It issues currency notes, acts as banker to the government, and supervises commercial banks.
Remember an important rule: the RBI does not open savings accounts for ordinary citizens. Commercial banks, cooperative banks and post offices serve households and businesses directly.

board.text: Commercial banks serve people; RBI regulates banks

text.en: How do commercial banks earn income? Suppose a bank pays four percent interest on your savings deposit and charges nine percent interest on a business loan.
The difference between the interest charged to borrowers and the interest paid to depositors is the bank's main source of income, which pays staff and keeps branches running.
Banks keep only a small fraction of deposits as cash reserve for daily withdrawals and lend the rest to farmers, shopkeepers and factories, helping the whole economy grow.
Now let us compare formal and informal sources of credit. Formal credit comes from commercial banks, regional rural banks and cooperative societies supervised by the RBI.
Informal credit comes from moneylenders, traders, landlords, friends or relatives. No central regulator monitors informal interest rates, which can sometimes be painfully high.
Formal loans usually ask for terms of credit: an agreed interest rate, repayment schedule, documentation, and sometimes collateral—an asset like land, gold or a vehicle pledged as security.

When credit helps a tailor buy a sewing machine and earn higher monthly income, it plays a positive role. When a failed crop forces a borrower to take a new loan to pay an old one, it creates a debt trap.
Poor families often lack formal collateral. Self-Help Groups solve this by pooling small regular savings from fifteen to twenty women in a neighbourhood.
After saving regularly for a year or two, the group becomes eligible for a low-interest bank loan without individual collateral, because the group shares responsibility for repayment.
In Tamil Nadu, women's Self-Help Groups supported through Mahalir Thittam have helped lakhs of families launch tailoring, dairy, catering and craft micro-enterprises.
Digital banking and Jan Dhan accounts have brought millions of previously unbanked citizens into the formal financial system, making direct benefit transfers transparent and fast.
Safe digital habits matter too: never share your PIN, OTP or CVV with anyone, and always check bank alerts to guard against online fraud.

board.text: Digital safety: never share PIN or OTP

text.en: Inflation happens when general prices rise and each rupee buys less than before. The RBI adjusts interest rates and credit supply to keep prices reasonably stable.

board.text: RBI controls credit to curb inflation

text.en: Smart money habits—saving regularly, borrowing from formal low-interest sources only for productive needs, and repaying on time—build lasting family security.

problem.en: A weaver needs ₹20,000 to buy yarn for a festival order. Compare borrowing from a local moneylender at 36% per year versus a cooperative bank or SHG at 10% per year.

text.en: Calculate the annual interest cost of each option.

why.en: At 36%, interest is ₹7,200 per year; at 10%, interest is only ₹2,000 per year.

text.en: Compare the risk of a debt trap.

why.en: High informal interest eats up most of the weaver's profit and can trap the family in debt if sales slow down.

text.en: Choose the safer credit source.

why.en: Formal credit through a cooperative bank or SHG keeps ₹5,200 more with the weaver and encourages steady business growth.
